lessons.title: Where Do Plant Wastes Go? Gum, Droplets and Falling Leaves

quiz.prompt: On a humid early morning, Grade 11 learners looked closely at grass and arrowroot (taro) leaves in the school garden. What did they see standing along the edges of the leaves?
choices: Yellow leaves dropping off
Thick milky sap oozing out
Amber resin that had hardened into a seal
Small droplets of liquid
quiz.rationale: Droplets of liquid along the leaf edges were the observation on grass and arrowroot leaves. Milky sap and resin came from cut Acacia or Euphorbia stems, and yellow leaves were seen fallen under trees.
quiz.placement: Nature Walk: droplets on the edges of grass and arrowroot leaves

quiz.prompt: During Think-Pair-Share, a learner predicts: 'The sticky sap from a cut Acacia is the plant's blood.' At this point in the lesson, what is the best scientific way to treat this idea?
choices: Record it as a prediction and test it later using evidence
Reject it at once because the teacher has not agreed with it
Ignore it because predictions made before teaching do not matter
Accept it as true because a classmate said it
quiz.rationale: A prediction is an idea that can be tested and revised. Predict-Observe-Explain asks learners to commit to an idea first and check it with evidence later.
quiz.placement: Think-Pair-Share of the comparative diagrams and the prediction 'I think a plant gets rid of its wastes by...'

quiz.prompt: A chart compares a running goat with a maize plant of the same body mass. It shows that the goat uses much more oxygen and food and makes much more nitrogenous waste. What does the chart show about the amount of nitrogenous waste the maize plant makes?
choices: The same amount as the goat
Much less than the goat
None at all
More than the goat
quiz.rationale: The chart shows that plants have a much lower metabolic rate and make much less nitrogenous waste per kilogram than animals. It does not show that plants make none.
quiz.placement: Step 2: annotating the chart comparing plant and animal metabolic rates

quiz.prompt: Excretion is the removal of metabolic wastes from the body. Which of these is an example of excretion in a human?
choices: Removing urea in urine
Breathing in oxygen
Swallowing food
Passing out undigested ugali fibre as faeces
quiz.rationale: Urea is a metabolic waste made inside body cells, so removing it in urine is excretion. Undigested fibre was never part of metabolism, so its removal is egestion, not excretion.
quiz.placement: Step 1 brainstorm on metabolic wastes and the introduction of the term excretion (excretion versus egestion)

quiz.prompt: After the debate, a learner says: 'We now have ideas about why plants have no kidneys, but we still cannot say what the droplets on the edges of arrowroot leaves are or how they form.' Which statement is correct at this stage of the unit?
choices: The plant is sick and is leaking liquid
The droplets are sweat from sweat glands on the leaf
How the droplets form has not been explained yet and will be investigated in the next lesson
The droplets are urine made by tiny kidneys inside the leaf
quiz.rationale: The lesson deliberately leaves the leaf-edge droplets unexplained. Learners name this as a gap to investigate in Lesson 2, and the other choices are untested misconceptions.
quiz.placement: Structured debate 'Plants do not need kidneys' and the gaps still unexplained, such as the leaf-edge droplets

quiz.prompt: Learners are writing sticky-note questions for the Driving Question Board about oozing sap, leaf-edge droplets and falling leaves. Which question best fits the board, because it is about the phenomenon and cannot be answered yet?
choices: Did we go on a nature walk today?
How many leaves does one arrowroot plant have?
What colour is the gum from an Acacia?
Why do arrowroot leaves have water drops along their edges in the morning?
quiz.rationale: A good DQB question starts with How or Why and asks about the phenomenon, and learners cannot yet answer it. The other questions can be answered by looking, counting or recalling.
quiz.placement: Driving Question Board: writing and clustering sticky-note questions

quiz.prompt: While revising her drawing, a learner puts a question mark on the arrow showing how wastes leave the plant, because she cannot explain it yet. Why is this a good scientific move?
choices: It means she did not take part in the lesson
It shows a gap in her model that needs to be investigated
It shows the drawing is completely wrong and must be rubbed out
It means the teacher will give the answer without any investigation
quiz.rationale: Marking unexplained routes with a '?' turns gaps into questions for investigation. It makes the growth in her thinking visible, and it prepares the next lesson's puzzle.
quiz.placement: Revising the Day 1 comparative diagram with a different coloured pen and marking '?' on routes not yet explained

lessons.title: How Do Plants Get Rid of Wastes? Nature Walk, Exudation and Guttation Evidence

quiz.prompt: On an early humid morning, a student says, "The droplets along the edges of the arrowroot leaf are just dew." Which observation would best suggest that the droplets come from the plant itself?
choices: The droplets are clear and have no colour
The droplets are seen only in the morning
The droplets are in the same places along the leaf margins and tips, not spread randomly over the leaf
The droplets are wet when touched
quiz.rationale: Guttation droplets form at hydathodes, which are fixed spots at leaf margins and tips. Dew settles randomly over the whole surface, so droplets at the same spots suggest the plant is releasing them.
quiz.placement: Predict: prediction on whether droplets on arrowroot leaf edges are waste, water or something else

quiz.prompt: A teacher makes a tiny cut on a Euphorbia stem. Thick white milky liquid oozes out and dries to cover the cut. Which waste-removal route does this show?
choices: Exudation of latex through a cut
Diffusion of gases through lenticels
Transpiration through stomata
Guttation through hydathodes
quiz.rationale: Gums, resins and latex that ooze out through cuts or bark are exudates, so this is exudation. Guttation gives watery droplets at leaf edges, and transpiration loses water vapour.
quiz.placement: Part A, Nature walk: Station 2, Euphorbia latex from a tiny cut

quiz.prompt: During the nature walk, learners collect fallen yellow leaves and see leaf scars on a branch. Why can the falling of old leaves count as a way a plant gets rid of wastes?
choices: Leaves fall only because of the season, so wastes are not involved
Wastes stored in the old leaves are removed from the plant when the leaves drop
Falling leaves reduce transpiration by closing the stomata
Falling leaves release gum and latex through the leaf scar
quiz.rationale: Plants can store wastes in old leaves, bark and fruits. When these parts fall, the stored wastes leave the plant. Seasonal leaf fall is not just a timing event.
quiz.placement: Part A, Nature walk: Station 4, fallen yellow leaves and leaf scars as evidence of tissue/organ fall

quiz.prompt: In the guttation experiment, one well-watered seedling is covered with a bell jar. A second seedling is left uncovered in a drier spot. What is the purpose of the uncovered seedling?
choices: To show that seedlings do not need water
To compare and show whether high humidity makes guttation droplets appear
To measure how much water the covered seedling absorbs
To make sure the covered seedling gets enough light
quiz.rationale: The control differs only in humidity. Comparing the two seedlings shows whether high humidity causes droplets at the leaf edges.
quiz.placement: Part B, Guttation experiment (POE): bell jar seedling and labelled control seedling

quiz.prompt: Guttation droplets form at leaf edges on a cool, humid night after the soil has been watered well. Which explanation is correct?
choices: The leaves sweat to cool down, as humans do
Roots absorb water faster than transpiration can remove it in humid air, so liquid water is forced out at hydathodes
The stomata open wide and release a lot of water vapour
Dew from the air falls and collects on the leaf edges
quiz.rationale: In humid air, transpiration is slow while the roots keep absorbing water. The extra water, with dissolved salts and sugars, is pushed out as liquid at hydathodes.
quiz.placement: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER): explaining the droplets at leaf tips under the jar

quiz.prompt: Which statement correctly contrasts guttation and transpiration?
choices: Guttation loses liquid water with dissolved substances through hydathodes, mainly at night or early morning. Transpiration loses water vapour through stomata, mainly in the day.
Guttation releases gum and resin from cuts, while transpiration releases latex.
Guttation loses water vapour through stomata in the day. Transpiration loses liquid water through hydathodes at night.
Guttation and transpiration both lose only water vapour, but guttation happens in the roots.
quiz.rationale: Guttation is liquid water carrying dissolved salts and sugars from hydathodes, mainly in humid conditions at night or early morning. Transpiration is water vapour lost through stomata, mainly in warm, dry daytime conditions.
quiz.placement: Venn diagram contrasting guttation and transpiration; exit ticket 'Contrast guttation and transpiration in 2 sentences'

quiz.prompt: After the nature walk, groups write new questions on the Driving Question Board. Which question is about wastes that are neither gases nor liquids and cannot easily evaporate or ooze out?
choices: Why does Euphorbia latex dry quickly at a cut?
Who buys gum arabic, and for how much?
What happens to wastes that cannot evaporate or ooze out easily?
Why do guttation droplets appear mostly at night?
quiz.rationale: The unanswered question about insoluble wastes that cannot evaporate or ooze out is the one that leads to the next lesson. The other questions are about guttation, the market value of gum, and latex drying.
quiz.placement: DQB: sorting new questions into Gaseous, Liquid, Solid/insoluble wastes and Economic importance

lessons.title: Where Do the Wastes Go? Shedding Old Leaves and Locking Away Crystals

quiz.prompt: Plants have no kidneys. A student predicts where a plant keeps wastes that cannot dissolve in water, such as calcium oxalate crystals, tannins and resins. Which prediction fits what the lesson develops?
choices: They dissolve in water and leave the plant as sweat through the leaves
They are stored in the growing tips so the plant can reuse them quickly
Plants do not make any wastes, so there is nothing to store
They are stored in non-vital parts such as bark, old leaves, fruits and flowers, which are later shed
quiz.rationale: Insoluble wastes are deposited in non-vital organs that the plant can later shed. The other choices are misconceptions: all waste leaves as liquid, wastes sit in vital tissue, or plants have no waste.
quiz.placement: Predict: hardened Acacia gum and yellow leaf prediction (Think-Pair-Share)

quiz.prompt: A group examines slides of a young green mango leaf and an old yellow mango leaf under a light microscope. They count needle-shaped crystals in 3 fields of view for each leaf. Which result would support the idea that old leaves store wastes?
choices: The same number of crystals in both leaves, as all leaves hold equal wastes
Crystals only in the veins of the young leaf
More crystals in the young green leaf than in the old yellow leaf
More crystals in the old yellow leaf than in the young green leaf
quiz.rationale: Old, non-vital leaves accumulate stored insoluble wastes, so more crystals are expected in the old yellow leaf than in the young leaf.
quiz.placement: Part C: Microscopy, crystal count table for young and old leaves

quiz.prompt: In the leaf microscopy practical, learners add a drop of iodine to a second slide of leaf tissue. Why do they do this?
choices: To make the leaf tissue produce more crystals
To dissolve calcium oxalate crystals so they can be counted
To check for starch, which stains blue-black, so it is not mistaken for crystals
To kill the cells so the crystals become bigger
quiz.rationale: Iodine stains starch blue-black, which helps learners tell starch grains apart from crystals.
quiz.placement: Part C: Microscopy, iodine test on a second slide

quiz.prompt: A learner sees needle-shaped crystals in old leaf tissue. After adding a drop of ethanoic acid at the edge of the coverslip, the crystals do not dissolve. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: The crystals are probably sugar, because sugar never dissolves
The crystals are probably calcium oxalate, which does not dissolve in ethanoic acid
The crystals are probably starch, because they stain blue-black
The crystals are probably calcium carbonate, because they fizz in acid
quiz.rationale: Calcium oxalate crystals do not dissolve in ethanoic acid, whereas carbonate crystals fizz or dissolve in dilute HCl. Starch is identified with iodine, not acid.
quiz.placement: Part C: Microscopy, dilute acid test on a third slide

quiz.prompt: One group looks carefully at slides of an old leaf and finds no crystals in any field of view. What should the group do?
choices: Draw crystals anyway so their result matches the other groups
Throw away the slide and copy another group's results
Report honestly that no crystals were seen, record it as data, and look in other places such as the veins or the leaf edge
Decide that the old leaf stores no wastes at all
quiz.rationale: Honest reporting is essential, and 'no crystals' is still data. One negative slide does not show that the leaf has no stored wastes, so the group should look in other parts of the leaf.
quiz.placement: Part C: Microscopy, groups who see no crystals

quiz.prompt: Groups find more calcium oxalate crystals in old yellow leaves than in young leaves. Which reasoning best explains why leaf fall counts as excretion?
choices: Wastes are locked in a harmless solid form in tissue the plant no longer needs, and they are removed when the leaf falls
Leaf fall removes crystals from the young leaves, which are the main storage site
The crystals dissolve in the yellow leaf and leave as droplets at the leaf edges
Leaf fall only helps the plant to lose water vapour through stomata
quiz.rationale: Insoluble wastes are deposited as crystals in old, non-vital leaves. They do not harm living cells, and the plant removes them when the organ is shed, so no excretory organ is needed.
quiz.placement: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) statement on how plants get rid of insoluble wastes

quiz.prompt: Learners revise the class model of plant excretion. Which pair correctly matches a waste with how it is removed?
choices: Calcium oxalate crystals stored in old leaves: removed when the leaves are shed
Droplets at leaf edges (guttation): deposited as crystals in bark
Water vapour: removed when old leaves fall
Resin: breathed out through the stomata as a gas
quiz.rationale: Insoluble wastes such as calcium oxalate are deposited in non-vital organs and leave with them when shed. Water vapour leaves by transpiration, and guttation releases liquid droplets, not crystals.
quiz.placement: Revising the class model: adding deposition and tissue fall alongside diffusion, transpiration and guttation

lessons.title: Cash from Waste: Categorising Plant Excretory Products and Their Value in Kenya

quiz.prompt: During the field walk, a learner crushes a lemongrass leaf and smells a strong scent. Which type of plant excretory product is mainly responsible for this smell?
choices: Gums and resins
Essential oils
Latex
Tannins
quiz.rationale: Lemongrass and eucalyptus leaves hold essential oils in leaf glands, and crushing the leaf releases the scent. Tannins, latex and gums do not give this strong aromatic smell.
quiz.placement: Part A: field observation (crushing a lemongrass or eucalyptus leaf to smell the essential oil)

quiz.prompt: Which row correctly matches the plant excretory product with its type and plant source?
choices: Gum arabic - alkaloid - Acacia senegal
Papain - essential oil - papaya
Rubber - latex - Hevea
Quinine - tannin - Cinchona
quiz.rationale: Rubber is made from latex tapped from the Hevea tree. Gum arabic is a gum (not an alkaloid), quinine is an alkaloid (not a tannin), and papain is a latex product from papaya (not an essential oil).
quiz.placement: Part B: research cards and the table (Excretory product | Type | Plant source | Kenyan use)

quiz.prompt: A learner says, 'Latex from a rubber tree is the blood of the plant.' Which statement correctly describes latex?
choices: It is a fluid that carries oxygen around the plant
It is a milky fluid stored in special cells and vessels, and it is not blood
It is sugar solution made in the leaves and sent to the roots
It is water and minerals moving up from the roots
quiz.rationale: Plants have no blood. Latex is a milky fluid stored in special latex cells or vessels, and it is an excretory product that people use to make rubber and papain.
quiz.placement: Class master table and CER discussion (teacher corrects the 'latex is blood' misconception)

quiz.prompt: Complete the CER argument. Claim: Plant excretory products are valuable in Kenyan markets. Evidence: quinine from Cinchona bark, rubber from Hevea latex and gum arabic from Acacia. Which is the best reasoning?
choices: The products are valuable because they are the main food that plants make for growth
The products are valuable because they come only from plants that grow in Kenya
Plants store these products in tissues such as bark and latex vessels, and people use their chemical properties, such as treating malaria, sealing and sticking
The products are valuable because plants throw them away, so they are free and easy to collect
quiz.rationale: Good reasoning links the accumulation of wastes in plant tissues to the useful chemical properties humans exploit, such as antimalarial action, stickiness and sealing. The other options give wrong ideas about what the products are or why they are valuable.
quiz.placement: CER statement: 'Why are plant excretory products valuable in Kenyan markets?'

quiz.prompt: A group wants to move the DQB question 'Why is the sticky sap from the Acacia tree worth money?' to 'answered'. Which evidence from today best justifies the move?
choices: The sap oozes out only when the tree is cut, so it has no use
Acacia sap hardens into gum arabic, which collectors in Turkana and Marsabit sell, so a plant waste earns money
All liquids that come out of plants are sold in markets
Acacia trees have thorns and grow in dry areas of Kenya
quiz.rationale: The sap hardens into gum arabic, an excretory product that people collect and sell. This links the phenomenon directly to its economic value. The other options are unrelated or incorrect.
quiz.placement: Revisiting the Driving Question Board (moving a question to 'answered' with evidence)

quiz.prompt: A group is updating its class model of plant excretion. Which annotation is correct?
choices: Latex is made in the leaf glands
Gums and resins ooze out of stem wounds
Essential oils are stored in latex vessels in the stem
Tannins are found only in the root hairs
quiz.rationale: Gums and resins ooze from wounds in the stem, as seen with Acacia. Essential oils are held in leaf glands, latex is held in latex vessels and bark, and tannins are found in bark and leaves.
quiz.placement: Revising the class model: labelled arrows showing where excretory products end up, plus 'Value to people'

quiz.prompt: Which statement correctly contrasts guttation and transpiration in plants?
choices: Both are the loss of latex from cut stems, but they happen at different times of day
Guttation is loss of liquid water droplets from leaf edges (often on humid mornings), while transpiration is loss of water vapour, mainly through stomata
Guttation is loss of water vapour through stomata, while transpiration is loss of liquid droplets from leaf edges
Guttation happens only in old yellow leaves, while transpiration happens only in young leaves
quiz.rationale: Guttation releases liquid droplets along leaf edges, as seen on grass and arrowroot on humid mornings. Transpiration is the loss of water vapour, mainly through the stomata.
quiz.placement: Daily Exit Ticket: 'Contrast guttation and transpiration in 2 sentences'

lessons.title: Who Profits from Plant Wastes? Community Uses, Alkaloid Risks and the Final Explanation

quiz.prompt: Tea leaves from Kericho contain caffeine and miraa (khat) contains cathinone. Both are alkaloids. Which statement about alkaloids is correct?
choices: Some alkaloids are useful in small controlled doses but harmful when abused
All alkaloids are harmful and should never be used
Alkaloids are harmless and cannot cause addiction
Only alkaloids from tobacco and miraa can harm people
quiz.rationale: Alkaloids such as caffeine and quinine are useful in small doses, but misuse (for example of nicotine or miraa) leads to addiction and health problems. The dose and the abuse make the difference.
quiz.placement: Predict: six labelled stations and the question 'could any of them harm people?'

quiz.prompt: A farmer cuts the stem of a Euphorbia hedge and thick milky latex oozes out and later hardens. Which excretory process released the latex?
choices: Organ fall
Exudation
Transpiration
Guttation
quiz.rationale: Exudation is the release of products such as latex, gum and resin from plant tissues, especially from cuts. Guttation releases water droplets, transpiration loses water vapour and organ fall removes leaves.
quiz.placement: Observe: hand lens re-examination of the hardened Acacia gum lump and dried Euphorbia latex sample

quiz.prompt: In Nakuru, tanners soak animal hides in a solution made from the bark of Acacia or wattle trees. Which plant excretory product in the bark makes this possible, and what is it used for?
choices: Pyrethrum, used to make insecticide
Quinine, used to treat malaria
Tannins, used for tanning hides into leather
Caffeine, used to flavour drinks
quiz.rationale: Tannins stored in Acacia and wattle bark are used to tan hides. Caffeine is in tea and coffee, pyrethrum is an insecticide and quinine is a malaria medicine.
quiz.placement: Observe: portfolio presentation and gallery rotation (tannins in Acacia/wattle bark used for tanning hides in Nakuru)

quiz.prompt: Early in the morning, droplets of liquid water are seen along the edges of arrowroot (taro) leaves. Which statement correctly contrasts guttation with transpiration?
choices: Guttation loses water vapour through stomata, while transpiration loses liquid droplets through hydathodes
Guttation and transpiration are the same process and both happen only at night
Guttation removes sticky resin from cut stems, while transpiration removes fallen leaves
Guttation loses liquid water droplets through hydathodes at leaf edges, while transpiration loses water vapour mainly through stomata
quiz.rationale: Guttation is the loss of liquid water from hydathodes, often in humid early mornings. Transpiration is the loss of water vapour, mainly through stomata.
quiz.placement: Explain: CER matrix evidence (guttation droplets at the edges of arrowroot leaves at 6:30 am) and the Daily Exit Ticket

quiz.prompt: A learner asks, 'Why does a plant not need a kidney?' Which answer is the best scientific reasoning?
choices: Plants produce very toxic wastes that must be kept inside the cells at all times
Plants absorb all their wastes from the soil and release them through the roots
Plants have low metabolic rates and less toxic wastes, recycle CO2 and O2 between photosynthesis and respiration, and store other wastes in dead tissues
Plants do not produce any wastes
quiz.rationale: Plants make less toxic wastes, recycle gases between photosynthesis and respiration, and store wastes such as tannins and resins in dead tissues or lose them by organ fall, so they need no kidneys.
quiz.placement: Explain: CER matrix reasoning column (why plants lack excretory organs)

quiz.prompt: A group interviewed 12 households in their community. 7 of the 12 households said they use neem leaves to treat malaria or skin problems. What percentage of the households use neem?
quiz.rationale: Percentage = 7 ÷ 12 × 100 = 58.3%. The value 41.7% is the share that do not use neem (5 out of 12).
quiz.placement: Explain: CER matrix evidence column (interview data, 7 of 12 households use neem)

quiz.prompt: In Lesson 1, a learner drew a model showing that plants have no wastes. After Lessons 1-5, which is the correct revised idea for the final model?
choices: Plants have no wastes, so nothing needs to be removed
Plants produce wastes, but these have no use to people
Plants produce wastes, but all of them are removed through kidneys in the roots
Plants produce wastes, but they remove or store them in different ways, such as exudation, guttation, deposition and organ fall
quiz.rationale: The evidence shows that plants do produce wastes. They remove them by diffusion, transpiration, guttation and exudation, or store them in tissues and lose them by organ fall, and many have economic value.
quiz.placement: Model: comparing the Lesson 1 model with the Final Model using blue and red pens
